claims.text: Equiatomic MoNbTaW has higher high-temperature strength than binary W–50 at% Ta.
Equiatomic MoNbTaW has a lower high-temperature creep rate than binary W–50 at% Ta.
The multicomponent MoNbTaW alloy has greater atomic-scale lattice distortion than binary W–Ta.
Increased lattice distortion raises the activation-energy barrier for dislocation climb at elevated temperature.
Increased lattice distortion raises the activation-energy barrier for dislocation cross-slip at elevated temperature.
The MoNbTaW and W–50 at% Ta specimens can both be produced as single-phase BCC materials with matched grain-size distributions and low impurity levels.
Williamson–Hall X-ray diffraction peak-broadening analysis can quantify the relevant degree of atomic-scale lattice distortion.
Diffuse-scattering intensity can quantify the relevant degree of atomic-scale lattice distortion.
The increased barriers to dislocation climb and cross-slip enhance high-temperature yield strength.
The increased barriers to dislocation climb and cross-slip reduce steady-state high-temperature creep.
At 1000 °C, equiatomic MoNbTaW will have approximately 20% higher yield strength than W–50 at% Ta.
At 1000 °C, equiatomic MoNbTaW will have approximately 30% lower steady-state creep rate than W–50 at% Ta.
The proposed mechanism applies to BCC refractory alloys between 900 and 1100 °C with grain sizes of approximately 5–20 µm under inert atmosphere or vacuum.
The proposed relationship may cease to hold above 1200 °C because phase changes or oxidation may dominate.
A temperature-dependent creep study can be used to extract an activation energy for creep.
A yield-strength difference below 5% and a creep-rate difference below 10% would constitute lack of improved mechanical performance relative to the binary control.
